newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Retail detracts 0.3 pct pt from Australia GDP.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Retail detracts 0.3 pct pt from Australia GDP.

text.p: Australian retail trade performance detracted 0.3 percentage point from December quarter growth in GDP, Bureau of Statistics data issued on Tuesday show.
The bureau said December quarter retail trade was A$25.555 billion in the 1989/90 currency used in GDP estimates, compared with A$25.886 billion in the previous quarter.
The quarterly change, minus A$330 million, is minus 0.3 percent of quarterly GDP.
This is a much greater fall than economists had expected.
The percentage change in constant-price retail trade was minus 1.3 percent, compared with the median expectation of minus 0.5 percent that a Reuters survey of economists found on Friday.
The actual fall was bigger than even the largest expected fall in the survey -- 1.1 percent.
Forecasts for December quarter GDP growth, currently about 0.4 percent at this preliminary stage, are now expected to decline.
The bureau revised its September quarter constant-price estimates only very slightly -- a revision total of minus A$21 million (1989/90 currency) for the March, June and September quarters.
Retail trade is part of private consumption, the remainder of which economists generally expect to be stronger than retail.
Before Tuesday's surprisingly weak retail data, economists expected private consumption to contribute about 0.2 percentage points to GDP growth.

Consumption is a component of the expenditure-based estimate of GDP (GDP-E), which is averaged with income-based (GDP-I) and production-based (GDP-P) estimates to produce GDP-A, the focus of economic policy.
The GDP data itself is due for release on March 5.
The following table gives economists' average December quarter forecasts expressed as contributions to quarterly GDP growth and updated with today's data.
Note, however that economists disagree wildly at this preliminary stage in the GDP forecasting round.
Items marked with an asterisk are now backed, at least partially, by published data.
The analysis excludes minor items and GDP-P, which is difficult to forecast.
